item.title: An agent needs more than just code access. How we moved our team's process into hooks and gates
item.description:
Hi! My name is Valery Poctarev, I develop antifraud tools and am responsible for the user access control system at Avito. This material will be useful for those who are implementing agents in development and are faced with the fact that they forget processes. Spoiler: we made agents work predictably by moving control to the level of deterministic runtime constraints. Initially, it seems sufficient to write detailed instructions in AGENTS.md, add rules for clean code and mandatory tests, and give the agent access to the codebase. But in a complex context, an agent can easily forget or bypass the text rules in AGENTS.md. To ensure they are not ignored, the agent needs a team context layer and strict runtime gates that they physically cannot bypass. We in the Checks (Antifraud) team have assembled such a setup — af-checks-context. We are now rolling it out from my personal use to the entire team to quickly share context and automate process agreements. I'll tell you what we stumbled upon and why we had to clean it up at some point. Read more

item.title: AI Agents: Doing Useless Tasks Faster
item.description:
For the past six months, I've been observing the implementation of AI agents in companies, and now I'm encountering it directly. Two things about the promises of tenfold acceleration bother me. First, we buy a tool but keep the processes the same. A task that used to take 16 working hours now takes one. Reviews have also sped up: agents, CI, evals, a proper harness. Technically, everything is excellent. Then the result waits two weeks for approval. Because one person makes the decision, priorities conflict, and responsibility is spread across departments. If the process is garbage, an agent will help speed up individual parts of it. But the two weeks of waiting won't disappear on their own. To speed things up, you'll have to change authorities, remove unnecessary approvals, and deal with queues. Perhaps give agents more decision-making power—along with verification criteria and responsibility boundaries. Buying licenses isn't the end of this work. Second, we don't always understand why we're doing a task in the first place. Suppose we've restructured the process. Now everything is fast: from постановка to release. Only the released feature is needed by no one. Requirements are met. Automatic review passed. Tests are green. Ticket closed. But did the user get better? Did revenue increase? Did costs decrease? Did anyone check? If no one measures the effect, the team can produce garbage for months and show a beautiful dynamic of closed tasks. With agents, it's even more beautiful. Production has increased. The usefulness of what was produced remained outside the report. Has the AI race already started for you? Have you managed to restructure processes and see a business effect—or has only the volume of work done increased so far? Read more

item.title: From a Vulnerable Plugin to a Top Manager's Disk: How an AI Agent Attacks and How to Catch It
item.description:
An attacking AI agent had a task: to access the documents of a top manager in a small company through its corporate network. In a few hours, guided by operator prompts, it traveled from a vulnerable plugin on a web server, through a mail server and domain controller, to the top manager's host, and viewed the disk contents there. Along the way, it set up three tunnels on captured servers and proceeded through them. On the defense side, it was countered by a complex of ML/AI solutions that detected 14 out of 15 steps of this attack without relying on rules written for specific tools. My name is Alexey Potapov, I am a leading expert in product expertise at the Positive Technologies (PT ESC) security expert center. Above, I described our lab test: a RedTeam AI agent simulating attacker actions against our complex. In this article, I will explain what we used for defense, how the attack unfolded, and what the defense saw at each of the three stages. Read on.

item.title: Can You Trick an AI Detector: Experiments with Editing and Translation
item.description:
What was left out last time? In the article "About University AI Detectors: What They Can and Cannot Do. Unexpected Results of My Own Testing," I concluded that the current versions of DUMET, Antiplagiat, and GPTZero can correctly identify the author of a text, and I proposed a more effective approach for this purpose, based on assessing the proportion of human text instead of AI. However, at that stage of testing, I only used original/primary texts that were either not subjected to any refinement (my own texts and their generated "twins") or texts of unknown origin with detected mixed authorship. Meanwhile, currently, there are fewer and fewer student papers that AI has not participated in writing in one way or another - as a search engine, generator, translator, or editor. The workload for AI detectors is increasing, and with it, the number of complaints about detector assessments, voiced not only by negligent students but also by excellent ones. It is claimed, in particular, that even entirely human text can be assessed by detectors as having significant AI involvement. Particularly striking is the story of Angelina, a student from Kemerovo University, who "had to rewrite her thesis 13 times" until Antiplagiat assessed it as original. Unfortunately, all such claims are usually unsubstantiated - I would very much like to examine real cases and understand the exact reason for false positive AI assessments. Read more

item.title: From Prompts to Specifications: How I Organized Test Automation Development with AI Agents
item.description:
Imagine a common task: expanding REST API coverage with autotests. AI agents can now handle such tasks: they study existing code, add necessary client methods, write test scenarios, and return a ready implementation. At first glance, everything is fine. Tests are written, the code is neat, and pytest successfully collects new checks. But does this mean the task is truly completed? Not necessarily. For example, an agent might check that the API returns HTTP 400 for an incorrect request but fail to check the error body structure. Or it might confirm that a request to delete a Git tag was successful but not verify if the tag actually disappeared from the repository. Formally, the tests exist. They might even pass. But how much can they be trusted? I encountered this problem when I started actively delegating autotest development to AI agents. In this article, I will show how I managed to organize work using the Specification-Driven Development (SDD) methodology, through the OpenSpec framework with specialized AI agents. I will analyze real REST API testing tasks and explain why a successful test run doesn't mean the test isn't garbage. The material is primarily for those who are proficient with APIs, Python, pytest, test design, and have basic experience with LLMs, but haven't yet figured out how to organize work through specifications (SDD, OpenSpec), multi-agent orchestration, and role separation. Read more

item.title: Analyzing Metrica with an AI Assistant using a Metal Warehouse Example
item.description:
In the previous article, we persuaded a metal warehouse to update its website. Let's assume we succeeded: prices in text, assortment, a "Calculate Cost" form. Orders started coming in. A couple of months later, on a Monday, the director asks a simple question: "Why did fewer orders come from the website last week?" The answer lies in Yandex Metrica. However, the director doesn't use Metrica, the sales manager gets confused in it, and the contractor will send a report on Friday. For such cases, we've created an open-source MCP server: it connects Metrica to an AI assistant (Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and others), allowing questions to be asked in plain language. Below is an analysis based on a hypothetical metal warehouse. The numbers are invented for example, but the investigation process is typical. Read on.
